stem: A vendor delivers boxes of light bulbs under an f.o.b. destination contract. The front desk signs for and accepts them, and they sit against a wall. Later the customer finds many bulbs broken. The contract has no warranty. Who bears the loss?

options.text: The Government, because risk of loss passed to it on acceptance at destination
options.why: Under f.o.b. destination, risk passes on acceptance or delivery at destination, whichever is later (46.505(b)(2)). Acceptance is generally conclusive except for latent defects, fraud or gross mistakes (46.501).

options.text: The vendor, because the bulbs turned out broken
options.why: Damage after acceptance is the Government's risk unless it was a latent defect present at delivery.

options.text: The person who signed for them, personally
options.why: Employees acting within the scope of their jobs do not personally bear contract losses.

options.text: The customer who picked them up
options.why: The customer is part of the Government; the loss is the Government's.

stem: Government-furnished property is damaged while in a contractor's hands. Under which contract is the contractor generally NOT held liable for the loss?

options.text: A cost-reimbursement contract
options.why: Contractors generally are not liable under cost-reimbursement, T&M, labor-hour, or fixed-price contracts awarded on certified cost or pricing data (45.104(a)).

options.text: A firm-fixed-price contract awarded on adequate price competition
options.why: That fixed-price contract is not on the list, so the contractor generally bears the loss.

options.text: A commercial firm-fixed-price purchase order
options.why: Not on the list either.

options.text: Any contract, because GFP always stays at the Government's risk
options.why: Liability depends on contract type, and the Government can revoke its assumption of risk (45.105(b)).

stem: Who is ordinarily required to furnish the property needed to perform a Government contract?

options.text: The contractor
options.why: Contractors ordinarily furnish all property needed (45.102(a)). The Government provides property only when it is clearly in its interest and the other tests in 45.102(b) are met.

options.text: The Government, always
options.why: GFP is the exception, not the rule.

options.text: Whoever the requiring activity chooses
options.why: The contracting officer decides, under the 45.102(b) tests.

options.text: The Government, whenever the contractor says it cannot afford it
options.why: A contractor's inability or unwillingness to supply its own resources is not enough (45.102(c)).

stem: A nonconformance is likely to materially reduce the usability of the supplies for their intended purpose, but not to create a hazard. How is it classified?

options.text: Major nonconformance
options.why: Major: likely to result in failure or to materially reduce usability (46.101). Note: one of the class slides swapped minor and major; this is the correct definition.

options.text: Minor nonconformance
options.why: Minor means NOT likely to materially reduce usability, or a departure with little bearing on use.

options.text: Critical nonconformance
options.why: Critical means likely to cause hazardous or unsafe conditions or to prevent a vital mission.

options.text: Latent defect
options.why: A latent defect is one that could not be found by reasonable inspection; it is not a nonconformance class.

stem: When must the Government perform quality assurance at the source rather than at destination?

options.text: When inspecting anywhere else would need uneconomical disassembly or destructive testing, or special equipment exists only at the source
options.why: 46.402 lists the source cases, including Government inspection during performance being essential. Off-the-shelf items needing no technical inspection go to destination (46.403).

options.text: For every commercial off-the-shelf item
options.why: Off-the-shelf items with no technical inspection are inspected at destination.

options.text: Whenever the buy is at or below the SAT
options.why: Below the SAT, inspection is normally at destination (46.404).

options.text: When the services are performed at destination
options.why: Services performed at destination are inspected there.

stem: What is the difference between quality control and quality assurance?

options.text: Quality control is the contractor checking its own work to catch defects; Government quality assurance checks that the contractor's work and processes meet the contract
options.why: Contractors are responsible for controlling quality, and Government contract quality assurance verifies conformance before acceptance (46.401).

options.text: They are the same thing
options.why: Different owners and purposes.

options.text: Quality assurance is done by the contractor; quality control by the Government
options.why: It is the other way around.

options.text: Quality control happens only after acceptance
options.why: Contractor quality control happens during production and performance.

stem: After acceptance, the Government discovers a defect that could not have been found by reasonable inspection. What kind of defect is it, and does acceptance block a remedy?

options.text: A latent defect; acceptance is not conclusive for latent defects, fraud or gross mistakes amounting to fraud
options.why: Acceptance is final except for latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes, or rights under a warranty (inspection clauses such as 52.246-2).

options.text: A patent defect; acceptance blocks any remedy
options.why: Patent defects are obvious ones a reasonable inspection should catch; this one could not be found.

options.text: A minor nonconformance; the Government must keep it
options.why: Nonconformance classes describe severity, not whether acceptance is final.

options.text: A warranty defect, so only the warranty applies
options.why: The scenario says there is a defect that reasonable inspection could not find: a latent defect.

stem: A proposal arrives by hand two hours after the closing time. Before award, may you consider it?

options.text: Only if an exception applies, such as proof it was under Government control before the deadline or it was the only proposal received, and accepting it would not unduly delay the buy
options.why: Late proposals are not considered unless received before award, not unduly delaying the buy, and one of the 15.107(b)(1) exceptions applies. A late modification that makes a winning proposal more favorable can always be accepted.

options.text: Yes, any time before award
options.why: Timing alone is not enough; an exception must apply.

options.text: Yes, if the offeror is a small business
options.why: Size status is not a late-proposal exception.

options.text: Never, under any circumstances
options.why: The FAR does list exceptions.

stem: A contract specialist retires and you inherit an RFP that closed last week. Four offers are in the file. What do you check first?

options.text: The date and time each offer was received, so you consider only timely offers unless a late-offer exception applies
options.why: Only proposals received by the exact time are considered, unless a 15.107(b) exception applies. Receipt times are marked or recorded (15.108(a)).

options.text: Which offer has the lowest price
options.why: Timeliness comes first; a late offer may not be evaluated at all.

options.text: Which offeror the requiring activity prefers
options.why: Preference has no place in the evaluation.

options.text: Whether to cancel and resolicit
options.why: A change of specialist is no reason to cancel.

stem: When may an offeror withdraw its proposal?

options.text: By written notice at any time before award
options.why: Proposals may be withdrawn by written notice at any time before award (15.107(d)).

options.text: Only before the closing date
options.why: Withdrawal is allowed until award.

options.text: Never, once submitted
options.why: Offerors may withdraw before award.

options.text: Only with the contracting officer's approval
options.why: No approval is needed; written notice is enough.

stem: An offeror is excluded from the competitive range. How long does it have to request a preaward debriefing?

options.text: 3 days after receiving the notice of exclusion, in writing
options.why: The request is due within 3 days (15.206-2(a)(1)). The offeror may ask to delay the debriefing until after award, which can affect protest timeliness.

options.text: 5 days after award
options.why: Award-related timing applies to postaward debriefings.

options.text: 10 days after the notice
options.why: Too long.

options.text: Any time before contract completion
options.why: Debriefing requests have short deadlines.

stem: What is the difference between a postaward orientation and a postaward debriefing?

options.text: An orientation is held with the winning contractor to align on how the contract will run; a debriefing explains the evaluation to offerors who request one
options.why: Postaward orientation conferences are a contract administration function (42.302(a)(3)). Debriefings explain the basis for selection to offerors (15.301-1).

options.text: They are the same meeting
options.why: Different audiences and purposes.

options.text: Debriefings are for the winner; orientations are for the losers
options.why: Orientations are with the awardee; any offeror, including the awardee, may request a debriefing.

options.text: Orientations replace debriefings for small businesses
options.why: No such rule exists.

stem: What must a postaward debriefing NOT include?

options.text: Point-by-point comparisons of the debriefed offeror's proposal with other offerors' proposals
options.why: Debriefings must not compare proposals point by point or reveal trade secrets, confidential cost data or names of past performance references (15.301-1(d)).

options.text: The overall evaluated price and technical rating of the winner
options.why: Those must be included (15.301-1(c)(1)(ii)).

options.text: A summary of the rationale for award
The significant weaknesses or deficiencies in the offeror's own proposal

stem: Under the RFO, what should a contracting officer do first on learning that a protest was filed on one of their buys?

options.text: Consult legal counsel, and for an agency protest notify the head of the contracting activity
options.why: Consult your designated legal advisor (33.103(a)) and notify the HCA as soon as practicable (33.104-4(a)(4)(ii)). Then follow the award and performance suspension rules.

options.text: Award the contract quickly before the protest is decided
options.why: Award is generally withheld pending an agency protest unless justified in writing (33.104-2(b)).

options.text: Call the protester to argue the case
options.why: Coordinate with counsel first.

options.text: Ignore it until GAO calls
options.why: Protests have tight deadlines.

stem: A vendor thinks the evaluation criteria in an open RFP are unfair. When must it protest?

options.text: Before the closing date for receipt of proposals
options.why: Protests of apparent solicitation improprieties must be filed before bid opening or the closing date (33.104-2(a)); GAO's rule is the same.

options.text: Within 10 days after award
options.why: Waiting until after award makes a solicitation protest untimely.

options.text: Within 5 days after a debriefing
options.why: That timing applies to issues learned in a required debriefing.

options.text: Any time before performance starts
options.why: Solicitation defects must be raised before closing.

stem: How long does an agency try to take to resolve an agency-level protest, and how long does GAO take?

options.text: Agency: best efforts within 35 days; GAO: within 100 days
options.why: Agencies make their best efforts to resolve protests within 35 days (33.104-4(c)(1)); GAO decides within 100 days (65 for express option).

options.text: Agency: 100 days; GAO: 35 days
options.why: Reversed.

options.text: Both within 30 days
options.why: Not the rule.

options.text: There are no time goals
options.why: Both have time goals.

stem: Is alternative dispute resolution (ADR) required in contract disputes?

options.text: No, it is voluntary; the Government's policy is to try to resolve issues by agreement at the contracting officer's level
options.why: ADR means procedures voluntarily used to resolve issues in controversy (33.201). Policy is to resolve disputes by mutual agreement where possible (33.204).

options.text: Yes, it is required before any claim
options.why: ADR is voluntary.

options.text: Yes, but only for claims over $100,000
options.why: Dollar value does not make ADR mandatory.

options.text: It is not allowed in DoW
options.why: DoW uses ADR, including at the ASBCA.

stem: When must a contractor certify a claim?

options.text: When it seeks payment of more than $100,000
options.why: A written demand for more than $100,000 is not a claim under the Contract Disputes statute until it is certified (2.101, 33.205-2).

options.text: For every claim, regardless of amount
options.why: Certification applies over $100,000.

options.text: Only for claims over $2.5 million
options.why: That figure is the FAR certified cost or pricing data threshold, not claims.

options.text: Never; only the Government certifies
options.why: The contractor certifies its own claim.

stem: How long must the agency keep a contract file after final payment?

options.text: 6 years after final payment
options.why: Contracts and related records, including successful and unsuccessful proposals, are kept 6 years after final payment (Table 4-3).

options.text: 3 years after award
options.why: Three years applies to certain construction payroll records, measured from completion.

options.text: Until the contracting officer leaves
options.why: Retention is set by rule, not by people.

options.text: Forever
options.why: Records follow the retention table and NARA schedules.

stem: A firm-fixed-price contract (not simplified procedures) is physically complete. Within what time should its file be closed?

options.text: Within 6 months after the contracting officer gets evidence of physical completion
options.why: FFP: 6 months. Contracts needing indirect rate settlement: 36 months. All others: 20 months. Simplified acquisitions are closed on evidence of receipt and final payment (Table 4-2).

options.text: Within 20 months
options.why: 20 months is for all other contracts.

options.text: Within 36 months
options.why: 36 months is for contracts requiring settlement of indirect cost rates.

options.text: Immediately on delivery
options.why: Closeout follows physical completion and the closeout checks.

stem: A DoW competitive solicitation that allowed 20 days for responses drew only one offer. What does the DFARS generally require?

options.text: Resolicit for at least 30 more days, unless an exception applies
options.why: DFARS 215.371-2 requires resoliciting for an additional period of at least 30 days when competitive procedures drew only one offer and the solicitation allowed fewer than 30 days, unless an exception or waiver applies. The DoW RFO deviation for Part 14 points to the same procedure.

options.text: Award to the single offeror immediately as adequate price competition
options.why: For DoW, one offer is not adequate price competition (FAR 15.403-2(c)(1)).

options.text: Cancel the requirement
options.why: Resoliciting is the normal step.

options.text: Convert to a sole-source contract without a justification
options.why: Any sole-source award still needs proper authority.

stem: Under the RFO, must contracting officers apply FAR Part 19 (small business) to buys performed outside the United States?

options.text: They must apply it inside the United States and its outlying areas, and may apply it outside
options.why: The RFO changed this: Part 19 must be applied in the U.S. and outlying areas and may be applied outside (19.000(b)(1)). Before the RFO, Part 19 applied only inside the U.S. Ask your policy office how DoW and your command apply it overseas.

options.text: Yes, it must always be applied overseas
options.why: Overseas application is permitted, not required.

options.text: No, Part 19 can never be used overseas
options.why: That was the old rule; the RFO now allows it.

options.text: Only for 8(a) awards
options.why: The rule covers the whole part.

verify: DoW and Army policy on applying Part 19 overseas under the RFO

stem: A noncommercial requirement is valued above the micro-purchase threshold but at or below the SAT. What does the RFO say about small business?

options.text: It must be set aside for small business concerns (see Part 19)
options.why: 13.102: acquisitions above the MPT and at or below the SAT must be set aside for small business, following Part 19's rules.

options.text: Small business rules do not apply below the SAT
options.why: That is the range where the set-aside reservation applies.

options.text: It must go to the 8(a) program
options.why: 8(a) is one option, not the rule.

options.text: It is up to the requiring activity
options.why: The contracting officer applies the rule.

stem: What is an organizational conflict of interest (OCI)?

options.text: When a firm's other activities or relationships make it unable to give impartial advice, impair its objectivity, or give it an unfair competitive advantage
options.why: That is the 2.101 definition. Subpart 9.5 covers identifying, evaluating and resolving OCIs.

options.text: When a Government employee owns stock in a contractor
options.why: That is a personal conflict of interest, covered by ethics rules (Part 3 and 5 CFR 2635).

options.text: When two offerors team up
options.why: Teaming is allowed and not an OCI by itself.

options.text: When a contractor protests
options.why: A protest is not a conflict of interest.

stem: May a Government employee solicit a gift from a contractor that does business with the agency?

options.text: No; employees may not solicit or accept, directly or indirectly, gratuities or anything of monetary value from such firms, except as ethics rules allow
options.why: 3.101-2 points to the standards of conduct (5 CFR 2635). Soliciting is never allowed; accepting is limited to narrow exceptions.

options.text: Yes, if it is worth less than $20
options.why: Soliciting is prohibited regardless of value; the small-gift exception applies only to unsolicited gifts.

options.text: Yes, after the contract is awarded
options.why: Award does not change the rule.

options.text: Yes, if the supervisor approves
options.why: A supervisor cannot approve soliciting gifts.

stem: Under the Prompt Payment Act, when is a proper invoice normally due for payment?

options.text: 30 days after receipt of a proper invoice or Government acceptance, whichever is later; DoW also aims to pay small businesses within 15 days
options.why: The standard due date is 30 days. Accelerated payment to small businesses with a goal of 15 days is a policy (32.009), not a new Prompt Payment Act deadline (32.009(b)).

options.text: 15 days for every contractor
options.why: 15 days is a goal for small businesses, not the standard due date.

options.text: 60 days after delivery
options.why: Not the rule.

options.text: Whenever funds become available
options.why: Late payments earn interest automatically.

stem: A small business asks for advance payments on a firm-fixed-price contract. What should you do first?

options.text: Look at other financing first: advance payments are the least preferred method
options.why: The order of preference is private financing, customary financing, loan guarantees, unusual financing, and then advance payments (32.106). Advance payments are authorized sparingly.

options.text: Reject the request outright
options.why: Advance payments are allowed in some cases; consider the options.

options.text: Approve it because it is a small business
options.why: Size status does not override the order of preference.

options.text: Pay the full price at award
options.why: That is not contract financing; it is a prepayment the FAR does not allow.

stem: A contracting officer awarded a $5.5 million contract instead of a $4 million offer from another firm. Which approach did the RFP most likely use?

options.text: Tradeoff: the higher-rated proposal's benefits were judged worth the extra cost
options.why: Only a tradeoff (or the highest-technically-rated approach) allows paying more for better non-price merit, and the decision must explain why the benefits merit the cost (15.205).

options.text: Lowest price technically acceptable
options.why: LPTA must award to the lowest-priced acceptable proposal.

options.text: Sealed bidding
options.why: Sealed bidding awards on price and price-related factors only.

options.text: Simplified procedures with no evaluation factors
options.why: Without stated factors, the higher price could not be justified.

stem: Who is the source selection authority (SSA) under the RFO if the agency head appoints no one else?

options.text: The contracting officer
options.why: A contracting officer is the SSA unless the agency head appoints another person (15.201(a)). The SSA selects the best value and may reject all proposals.

options.text: The program manager
options.why: Only if appointed.

options.text: The technical evaluation chair
options.why: Evaluators advise; they do not decide.

options.text: The competition advocate
options.why: The advocate promotes competition; it does not select sources.

stem: Under the RFO, when must agencies conduct market research?

options.text: Before developing new requirements, before soliciting offers over the SAT, and before awarding a task or delivery order over the SAT
options.why: 10.001(b) lists the three triggers. Exchanges with industry are encouraged any time from identifying the need through receipt of proposals (15.101(a)).

options.text: Only after award
options.why: Market research shapes the requirement and strategy before award.

options.text: Only for buys over $10 million
options.why: The trigger is the SAT.

options.text: Only when competition is expected to be limited
options.why: It is required for every new requirement.

stem: For a dollar threshold, do you count the value of options in a base-plus-four-option-years contract?

options.text: Yes, thresholds use the final anticipated value including all options
options.why: 1.107(c). The amount you obligate at award is different; the threshold test uses the total including options.

options.text: No, only the base year counts
options.why: Counting only the base year would let buys dodge thresholds.

options.text: Only options the Government expects to exercise
options.why: All options count.

options.text: Only for construction
options.why: The convention applies to every buy.

stem: Must every modification to a commercial contract under 52.212-4 be bilateral?

options.text: Changes to the terms and conditions need written agreement of both parties, but administrative changes and actions under other clauses, such as exercising an option, can still be unilateral
options.why: 52.212-4(d) says changes to the terms may be made only by written agreement. Administrative changes do not change substantive rights (43.201), and option clauses give a unilateral right.

options.text: Yes, even an address correction needs the contractor's signature
options.why: An administrative change does not change the terms.

options.text: No, commercial contracts use the Changes clause like any other contract
options.why: 52.212-4 has no unilateral changes clause.

options.text: Commercial contracts cannot be modified
options.why: They can, by written agreement.

stem: A subcontractor complains it has not been paid and calls you to demand payment. What is the Government's relationship with the subcontractor?

options.text: There is no privity of contract; the subcontractor must look to the prime contractor
options.why: The Government contracts with the prime only. Subcontractors deal with the prime, though you can check the prime's compliance with its payment duties.

options.text: The Government must pay the subcontractor directly
options.why: That would pay twice and ignore privity.

options.text: The subcontractor can file a claim with the contracting officer
options.why: Only parties to the contract can bring Contract Disputes claims.

options.text: The subcontractor can file a bid protest
options.why: Protests concern awards, not payment.

stem: The requiring activity needs a fourth production lot of a mature missile with stable design and good cost history. Which contract type fits best?

options.text: Firm-fixed-price
options.why: When risk is minimal or predictable and you can set a fair price at the outset, use FFP (16.102(c), 16.202-2). A fourth production lot is mature.

options.text: Cost-plus-fixed-fee
options.why: Cost-type is for undefined or highly uncertain work, not mature production.

options.text: Time-and-materials
options.why: T&M is for work whose extent cannot be estimated, not production lots.

options.text: Letter contract
options.why: Letter contracts are for urgent starts before terms are set.
